license: Our own (story text written for Waymark)

data.title: The Stranger at the Gate
data.intro: Dusk, and dust on someone’s boots. A stranger stands at the gate, looks up at the words painted over the arch, and can’t read them. The innkeeper has her hands in the dough. She looks at you.
data.rules: Three parts, as the innkeeper asks. Read a page of her guest book: say what each line means. Write the stranger’s name on the slate, from memory. Then tell the whole table the story of your road, in Arabic, at least 6 of your lines. A judge reads the chat for three things: you understood, you answered, you kept it going. It can’t hear you, so it never judges your pronunciation.
data.book: The innkeeper wipes her hands and opens the guest book to a page in her own hand. “Read it to them,” she says, and nods at the stranger.
data.slate: The stranger tells you their name. The scribe slides the slate across the table: the guest book wants it in Arabic.
data.story: “Now,” says the innkeeper, pulling out the bench, “tell them how you got here.” The whole table turns to listen.
data.screen: The full table at night, every regular’s keepsake in its place: Salim’s cup, Nasser’s map, Leila’s portrait over the table. The stranger sits on the bench, and the guest book lies open.
data.epilogue: You say what was said to you. “You can’t read the signs on the road? Then sit. Every traveler starts with a few letters.” The innkeeper opens her book to a clean page and, this time, hands you the pen.
data.missed: The stranger smiles and stays the night anyway. The innkeeper says you can try again whenever you like: the table isn’t going anywhere.
